The old 100-emails-a-day free tier is gone, replaced by a 60-day trial that forces you onto a paid plan — and the entry-level Essentials plan now starts at $19.95/month. Add the recurring complaints about slow support, shared-IP deliverability dips, and surprise account suspensions, and it’s no surprise developers and marketers are searching for a way out. Reddit threads with titles like “SendGrid is over, what to use instead?” tell the whole story. If you’re only choosing between SendGrid and Mailgun, our [SendGrid vs Mailgun](https://www.mailercloud.com/blog/sendgrid-vs-mailgun) comparison scores them round by round. We compared 12 SendGrid alternatives across five criteria: pricing, deliverability, API and SMTP quality, ease of use, and support. For pure high-volume developer sending, Amazon SES, Postmark, and Mailgun are also strong picks. Here’s the full breakdown. **Quick Answer:** **Mailercloud is the best SendGrid alternative in 2026** — starting at $7/month with a real free plan (1,000 contacts, 12,000 emails/month) that SendGrid scrapped when it killed its free tier. web.title: 7 Best Transactional Email Services in 2026 (Compared) - Venture Harbour
web.description:
I first wrote this comparison in 2014, after spending many hours helping a client choose a transactional email system for their invoices, receipts, and password resets. Twelve years on, I still get emails about it — so I’ve rewritten it from scratch for 2026, based on what we currently use across our own ventures.

The category has changed a lot. Mandrill effectively removed itself from contention, SendGrid killed its free plan, and a newer generation of developer-first tools — Resend in particular — has made the incumbents look a bit sleepy.

**Short on time?** Postmark is the most reliable option if deliverability speed matters (we use it for TrueNorth). Resend is the best pick for developers — 3,000 free emails/month via a genuinely pleasant API. Brevo is the best free tier and the only tool here that also handles [marketing email](https://ventureharbour.com/email-marketing-software-tools-one-best/) properly. Amazon SES is the cheapest at scale, if you can stomach the setup.

### The Best Transactional Email Services in 2026
| Service | Best for | Free tier | Price from |
|-|-|-|-|
| [Postmark](https://postmarkapp.com/) | Deliverability & speed | 100 emails/mo | $15/mo (10,000 emails) |
| [Resend](https://resend.com/) | Developers | 3,000 emails/mo | $20/mo (50,000 emails) |
| [Brevo](https://ventureharbour.com/recommends/sendinblue-transactional/) | Free tier + marketing email in one | 300 emails/day (~9,000/mo) | $0 |
| [Amazon SES](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/) | Lowest cost at scale | 3,000/mo (first 12 months only) | $0.10 per 1,000 emails |
| [SendGrid](https://sendgrid.com/) | High volume with support | None (60-day trial) | $19.95/mo (up to 100,000 emails) |
| [Mailgun](https://www.mailgun.com/) | Developer infrastructure | 100 emails/day | $15/mo (10,000 emails) |
| [Mailjet](https://ventureharbour.com/recommends/mailjet/) | Simple SMTP with a UI | 6,000/mo (200/day) | Free, paid plans above that |

## The Pros and Cons of Transactional Email Services
### Resend – 4.5/5
[Resend](https://resend.com/) is the newest tool here and the one I’d reach for first on any new project.

It’s built by developers for developers — the API is clean, the docs are excellent, and React Email support means your templates live in code rather than a clunky WYSIWYG editor. The free tier gives you 3,000 emails/month (capped at 100/day), and the Pro plan is $20/mo for 50,000 emails or $35/mo for 100,000 (verified July 2026). It’s the same tool I recommend to developers in my [email marketing software guide](https://ventureharbour.com/email-marketing-software-tools-one-best/).

The downsides are mostly about maturity. Resend hasn’t been through a decade of reputation management the way Postmark has, and they doubled several Scale-tier prices overnight in late 2024 — the 200,000/month tier went from $80 to $160. Fine if you’re on the lower tiers, but worth factoring in if you expect to scale hard on their infrastructure.

If you’re a developer starting something new in 2026, start here. If you’re sending mission-critical volume and deliverability speed is your whole business, Postmark still has the edge.

### Amazon SES – 3.5/5
When competing on price, it’s still hard to beat Amazon. At $0.10 per 1,000 emails (verified July 2026 — a rate that hasn’t moved in over a decade), [Amazon SES](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/) is by far the cheapest way to send email at scale. A million emails costs about $100.

The catch is everything else. The console is bare-bones, analytics are minimal, and getting out of the sandbox and through IP warm-up is a project, not an afternoon. Dedicated IPs cost extra ($24.95/mo standard, or managed IPs from $15/mo).

One change worth flagging: the old free tier of 62,000 emails/month for EC2-hosted apps is gone. New customers now get 3,000 messages/month free for the first 12 months only (verified July 2026), so SES is no longer the “free forever” option it used to be for production apps.

Consider SES the bare-bones option — if all you need is emails in inboxes at the lowest possible cost, and you have engineering time to spend, this is the way to go. If you don’t, you’ll pay for the savings in other ways.

### SendGrid – 3/5
[SendGrid](https://sendgrid.com/) is still the biggest name in transactional email, and since the Twilio acquisition it’s clearly oriented towards high-volume enterprise senders.

The big news: SendGrid retired its free plan in 2025. New users now get a 60-day trial of 100 emails/day, after which you’re on Essentials at $19.95/mo — which does cover up to 100,000 emails (verified July 2026), so it’s decent value at volume. It’s poor value if you’re sending 5,000.

The analytics remain good and deliverability at scale is solid. But back in 2014 I noted a pattern of smaller customers complaining they’d been deprioritised in favour of enterprise accounts, and a decade later that direction of travel has only continued — killing the free tier being the clearest signal yet.

If you’re sending 100,000+ emails/month and want a vendor with enterprise support, SendGrid earns its place. Below that, Resend or Postmark will treat you better.

### Mailgun – 3/5
My original research into [Mailgun](https://www.mailgun.com/) was underwhelming, and my updated view is only slightly warmer.

Mailgun’s pitch is developer infrastructure — APIs, routing, validation — and pricing is reasonable: the Basic plan is $15/mo for 10,000 emails, with a limited free tier of 100 emails/day (verified July 2026). It’s a competent, unexciting workhorse.

The problem is positioning. Resend beats it on developer experience, Postmark beats it on deliverability, and SES beats it on price. It’s now owned by Sinch (as is Mailjet, making them corporate siblings), and it doesn’t obviously lead in anything. Fine to use, hard to recommend over the alternatives.

### Mailjet – 2.5/5
My first impressions of [Mailjet](https://ventureharbour.com/recommends/mailjet/) in 2014 weren’t great — a company specialising in email responded to my email by pointing me at a web form. Over a decade later, my view has softened a little, but not much.

To its credit: the interface is pleasant, and the free tier of 6,000 emails/month (capped at 200/day, verified July 2026) is one of the more generous ongoing free options now that SendGrid has none. Exceed the daily cap and your emails queue rather than send — worth knowing if your volume is spiky.

The trouble is the same as it was in 2014: I struggle to name the situation where Mailjet is the _best_ choice. Brevo’s free tier is bigger and its platform broader; Resend’s developer experience is better. Mailjet is fine. “Fine” is rarely worth choosing.

## Updates
**July 2026:** Full modernisation of this post, which was originally written in 2014. Added Resend (which didn’t exist when this was first published), rewrote the Postmark, Amazon SES, SendGrid, Mailgun, and Mailjet sections with pricing verified against each provider’s site in July 2026, and noted SendGrid’s 2025 retirement of its free plan and the changes to Amazon SES’s free tier. Mandrill remains a cautionary tale.

Ask any developer forum which transactional email service to use, and the thread splits instantly. Mailtrap, Resend, and Postmark split the vote while SES defenders argue about total cost of ownership in the replies. There’s never a consensus because the question is wrong.

These providers serve the same function (sending password resets, invoices, and welcome emails) but optimize for different things. Mailtrap optimizes for keeping transactional and bulk email separated inside one account. Resend optimizes for developer experience. Postmark optimizes for deliverability. SES optimizes for cost at scale. The right pick depends on which of those matters most at the current stage of the product.

## Mailtrap: the stream separator
[Mailtrap](https://www.buildmvpfast.com/alternatives/mailtrap) runs transactional and bulk traffic on isolated infrastructure behind different host URLs, on every plan including the free tier, so the endpoint your code calls decides which reputation pool the message uses.

![Mailtrap homepage with the headline Modern Email Delivery for developer and product teams](https://www.buildmvpfast.com/images/blog/resend-vs-ses-vs-postmark-transactional-email-deliverability-saas-2026/mailtrap-homepage.webp)

The deliverability work is automated. Adding a sending domain generates its SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records and validates them, DKIM keys rotate without a manual DNS change, and suppression handling is built in. The Business plan bundles a dedicated IP with automated warmup instead of billing it as an add-on.

The developer surface is modern.

Mailtrap’s pricing sits between SES and Postmark. Free covers 4,000 emails a month with a 150-per-day cap and no expiry. Basic runs $15/month for 10,000 emails and $30 for 100,000, where Postmark costs roughly $50 and Resend $40. Business starts at $85/month for 100,000 with the dedicated IP, sub-accounts, and SSO.

**Where Mailtrap falls short:**

24/7 support starts on the Business plan. Lower tiers get email support on weekdays, and dedicated IP pools are available from the Business tier and above.

## Resend: the developer experience play
Resend keeps winning developer polls for a reason. The API is clean, the TypeScript SDK is well-typed, and the React Email integration means email templates can be written as React components, previewed locally, and version-controlled alongside the rest of the codebase.

![Resend homepage with the headline Email for developers and a dark, developer-focused landing page](https://www.buildmvpfast.com/images/blog/resend-vs-ses-vs-postmark-transactional-email-deliverability-saas-2026/resend-homepage.webp)

The free tier includes 3,000 emails/month and one custom domain, which covers most MVPs through their first few hundred users. For teams already in the React ecosystem, the onboarding friction is close to zero.

The React Email angle is worth expanding on. Traditional email template development involves writing HTML tables, testing across dozens of email clients, and maintaining separate template files disconnected from the main application code. React Email collapses that into component-based templates that render to email-compatible HTML. For teams already building in `Next.js`, the workflow is natural: write a component, preview it in the browser, send it through the Resend API.

**Where Resend falls short:**

The pricing curve gets steep at volume. At 1M emails/month, Resend costs roughly $600, six times what SES charges for the same volume. Multiple developers have reported billing surprises once their send volumes crossed a tier boundary, and at least one built an open-source alternative after email costs hit $200+/month.

Bounce handling for bulk sends is still rough compared to Postmark. A developer evaluating providers for a multi-tenant setup put it directly: “Resend has the best DX right now but their bounce handling for bulk is genuinely rough.” For pure transactional email at moderate volumes, this matters less. For products sending marketing emails alongside transactional ones, the gap is noticeable.

And there’s the maturity question. Resend is younger than both Postmark and SES. The developer experience is genuinely excellent, but newer means a smaller track record for edge cases at scale.

## Amazon SES: cheap until it isn’t
SES is the price leader and it’s not close. At $0.10 per 1,000 emails with no monthly base fee, the raw cost of sending email through SES is a fraction of what [Postmark](https://www.buildmvpfast.com/tools/api-pricing-estimator/postmark) or Resend charge. For a SaaS sending 100,000 emails/month, SES costs about $10. Resend costs $40. Postmark costs $50.

That price difference evaporates once the hidden costs surface.

**Production access requires approval.** SES starts every new account in sandbox mode, limited to sending only to verified email addresses. Moving to production requires a written request explaining the use case, expected volume, and bounce-handling strategy. One developer described multiple failed approval attempts before concluding “Amazon SES is a waste of time for smaller businesses.” Getting approved without significant billing history on other AWS services is notoriously difficult.

**Reputation management is self-service.** The trade-off is blunt: SES is cheaper, but you’re signing up for more deliverability and reputation work. SES provides the sending infrastructure but expects the sender to handle IP warmup, suppression lists, complaint feedback loops, and bounce processing. Skip any of these and deliverability degrades silently.

**The operational overhead is real.** An AWS engineer on r/AWS_cloud who uses Resend for their own SaaS explained the reasoning: “When I found out Resend runs on Amazon SES under the hood, it confirmed my view: email infrastructure is a pain, even when you know AWS well. Sometimes a specialized service is worth more than DIY.”

That last point deserves emphasis. Multiple providers (including Resend) run on SES infrastructure underneath. The question isn’t whether SES can deliver email reliably. It can. The question is whether building the reliability layer on top is a good use of engineering time for a given team.

## Postmark: the deliverability purist
Postmark takes a different approach from both Resend and SES. The platform only allows transactional email. No cold outreach. No marketing blasts. Every sender on the platform sends password resets, receipts, and notifications, which keeps Postmark’s shared IP reputation exceptionally clean.

![Postmark homepage with the headline The email delivery service that people actually like, alongside customer testimonials about deliverability](https://www.buildmvpfast.com/images/blog/resend-vs-ses-vs-postmark-transactional-email-deliverability-saas-2026/postmark-homepage.webp)

Developers who evaluate multiple providers for client work consistently land on Postmark when deliverability is the priority. One r/webdev commenter captured the sentiment: “If the client has the budget, I prefer Postmark. Their logs are top notch, makes troubleshooting a breeze, and support is great.”

The logging and support angle comes up repeatedly. When an email doesn’t arrive, Postmark’s activity feed shows exactly what happened: delivered, bounced, marked as spam, or deferred. SES provides similar data through CloudWatch and SNS, but assembling a useful debugging view requires building the dashboard. Resend’s logs exist but are less mature than Postmark’s.

**The transactional-only restriction is a feature and a limitation.** It keeps deliverability high because no sender on the platform is doing anything that damages IP reputation. But it means a SaaS that also needs to send [newsletters](https://www.buildmvpfast.com/blog/best-email-newsletter-tools-mvp-2026) or marketing emails needs a second provider for that stream. Postmark is rock solid for transactional precisely because it’s strict about mixing transactional and marketing streams. That strictness is a feature, not a bug.

**Pricing is mid-range.** Postmark’s $15/month entry tier covers 10,000 emails. At 100K/month, the cost is roughly $50. At 1M/month, approximately $700. More expensive than SES, comparable to [Resend](https://www.buildmvpfast.com/compare/resend-vs-sendgrid), and the premium buys deliverability and operational simplicity.

Hold on, one thing worth mentioning here. Postmark recently released a bulk API for broadcast sends, which softens the transactional-only limitation. Broadcast messages (product updates, changelogs) can now go through Postmark on a separate stream with its own IP pool. That’s a meaningful gap-closer for teams that previously needed a second provider.

## When to pick each one
**Pick Mailtrap when:** The product sends both transactional and bulk email and you would rather not run two providers, deliverability defaults matter more than template ergonomics, and per-provider delivery logs are worth having when something does not arrive.

**Pick Resend when:** The team builds in `Next.js` or React, developer experience matters more than per-email cost, volume is under 500K/month, and the product needs to ship quickly. The React Email integration, instant production access, and clean API make it the fastest path from zero to sending.

**Pick Amazon SES when:** Monthly volume exceeds 500K, the team already operates in AWS, dedicated engineers can build and maintain bounce handling, suppression lists, and [deliverability monitoring](https://www.buildmvpfast.com/blog/stripe-webhook-failures-silent-revenue-loss-monitoring-setup-2026), and per-email cost is a primary concern. SES is the right choice for teams that treat email infrastructure as an engineering problem worth solving.

**Pick Postmark when:** Deliverability is the top priority (password resets, two-factor codes, payment receipts), the team prefers operational simplicity over raw cost savings, and logging and support quality matter. Postmark is the right choice for SaaS products where a missed transactional email directly impacts revenue or user trust.

**The stage-based framework:**

**MVP (0–1,000 users):** Mailtrap free tier (4,000 emails/month) is one of the most generous, or Resend free tier (3,000 emails/month). Either covers early traction with zero cost and minimal setup.

**Growth (1,000–10,000 users):** Mailtrap ($15/month), Resend Pro ($20/month), or Postmark ($15/month). All three handle this volume. Pick based on whether running both email streams in one account (Mailtrap), DX (Resend), or deliverability logging (Postmark) matters more.

**Scale (10,000+ users, 500K+ emails/month):** Evaluate SES. The cost savings justify the engineering investment at this volume. Keep Mailtrap or Postmark as a fallback for critical transactional flows (password resets, payment confirmations) where deliverability cannot be compromised.
